title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions
authors: Kidus Abebe, David Gaetano, Aurelia Moriyama-Gurish, Jana Šmilauerová, Yanfei Gao, Udo D. Schwarz
abstract: Ti-15Mo (wt%) is a well-established $β$-stabilized alloy whose mechanical response is strongly governed by phase stability and deformation mechanisms that operate at the single-grain scale. Because these intragranular mechanisms are intrinsically anisotropic, understanding the orientation dependence of the elastic and plastic response is critical to the texture-engineered processing of wrought components. Here, we quantify the nanomechanical anisotropy of single-crystal Ti-15Mo by combining EBSD with nanoindentation to correlate hardness, indentation modulus, strain rate sensitivity, and indentation yield response with the crystallographic surface normal near $\langle111\rangle,\langle124\rangle,\langle011\rangle,\langle023\rangle$, and $\langle013\rangle$ directions. While the modulus anisotropy is small (~10%), contrary to the prediction for a cubic crystal with A>1, orientations near $\langle111\rangle$ exhibit the lowest moduli. Yield onset is likewise softest near $\langle111\rangle$ and spans 41%, while hardness spans only 6.6% and follows neither the modulus nor the yield ordering. The alloy also exhibits yield behavior not captured by the simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models evaluated here. Strain-rate-jump tests yield V*=18-31b$^3$, consistent with kink-pair-nucleation-controlled plasticity; based on V*, the orientations separate into two groups suggestive of glide-dominated versus twin/transformation-participating response. We reveal an inversion of the elastic anisotropy expected for a homogeneous cubic $β$-phase and an orientation-dependent yield-onset response that is not reproduced by the simple Schmid-factor models examined here. Retained athermal $ω$ is proposed as the contributor because $β\rightarrowω$ collapse occurs on {111}$_β$ planes and may provide anelastic compliance through the reversible $ω\rightarrowβ$ transformation.

infographic.key_insight: Single-crystal Ti-15Mo shows inverted orientation-dependent elasticity and yield onset, with <111>-near surfaces unexpectedly the softest and not explainable by simple Schmid-factor/CRSS predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Texture and grain orientation in Ti-15Mo can materially change local compliance and incipient plasticity, so processing routes must account for single-grain anisotropy when targeting reliable wrought-component performance.
method: EBSD-guided nanoindentation on surfaces near <111>, <124>, <011>, <023>, and <013> crystallographic normals
Measured indentation modulus, hardness, strain-rate sensitivity, and yield onset across orientations
Performed strain-rate-jump analysis to estimate activation volume and infer deformation mechanism groups
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports only ~10% modulus anisotropy, 41% spread in yield onset, 6.6% hardness spread, and activation volumes of 18–31 b^3 that separate the orientations into two response groups.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed retained athermal ω-phase explanation is inferential from indentation data, so direct phase/microstructure confirmation would be needed before using it as a design rule.
infographic.paper_title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions

title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
authors: Wenpu Du, Peng Zhou, Yunlong Xia, Sinuo Xin, Congcong Zhang, Boyang Zhang
abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: PC-GNO learns the full mid-plane six-component stress tensor field in concrete penetration by coupling graph message passing with physics-informed impedance-based interactions and spectral normalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables surrogate prediction of field-level impact response from design inputs alone, supporting faster penetration-resistant concrete assessment than aggregate-resolved FEM.
method: Train on 359 full-scale, aggregate-resolved FEM cases at 100, 135, and 165 m/s across 14, 23, and 48 MPa concrete strengths.
Build graph coupling strength from material impedance contrast across interfaces.
Predict the complete six-component tensor field in function space rather than a single scalar response.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was verified against laboratory measurements and achieved mean accuracy of 80.16% across the three levels, outperforming the preceding-frame field baseline and a linear regression benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is tied to the training/evaluation conditions, so generalization to other projectile types, geometries, or concrete mixes may require retraining or validation.
infographic.paper_title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration

title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
authors: Gang Liu, Chen Yang, Junyan Hu, Jianguo Chen, Lixin Duan
abstract: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

infographic.key_insight: LizTail lets a fixed systolic array adapt both its shape and its parallel execution layout by splitting the array into reconfigurable segments with only endpoint connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves utilization on irregular workloads like skinny CNN matrices and small-batch LLM decoding, where conventional fixed arrays waste compute and underuse available parallelism.
method: Partition a 128×128 array into 32 regular 128×4 segments.
Add only predefined endpoint links for trimming, turn-back extension, and distributed execution.
Use a hardware-constrained mapper to choose execution organization, dataflow, partitioning, and tiling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports geometric-mean speedups of 5.02× for CNN inference and 25.67× for LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, with EDP reductions up to 38.23×.
infographic.watch_item: The design depends on segmented reconfiguration and specialized buffers/control, so real hardware may face routing, timing, and implementation complexity tradeoffs.
infographic.paper_title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays

title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang, Jinyi Xu, Xinchao Wang
abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.

infographic.key_insight: LLM2R reformulates 3D part assembly as a single-pass sequence modeling problem, using an adapted decoder-only LLM to predict all rigid part poses jointly with global context.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves scalable assembly of fractured or disassembled parts in robotics, digital reconstruction, and CAD pipelines, especially as part counts grow.
method: Encode each part with Point-BERT + Q-Former into geometric token blocks
Concatenate all part tokens and process them with a causal LLM adapted by LoRA
Add learnable summary tokens plus a part-aware pose head to predict SE(3) transforms for every part in one forward pass
infographic.evidence_signal: The method reports top performance across three PartNet categories, PartNeXt, and Breaking Bad, with particularly large gains at 100 parts and strong zero-shot transfer to unseen categories.
infographic.watch_item: Because causal attention limits each part to earlier parts, performance may depend on part ordering and careful tokenization/summary-token design.
infographic.paper_title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers

title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee
abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.

infographic.key_insight: A small set of real measurements can validate a high-fidelity FEM model, which then generates enough synthetic data to train a real-time GNN surrogate for soft tactile deformation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables sub-millimeter tactile deformation prediction at millisecond speed, supporting virtual prototyping and simulator-based design without extensive fragile-sensor testing.
method: Validate an ANSYS FEM model using 82 camera-tracked real contact cases.
Generate 768 synthetic contact scenarios from the validated FEM for GNN training.
Use the GNN for both forward prediction and inverse inference of tactile deformation/contact localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The validated FEM achieved sub-0.5 mm error in over 90% of validation cases, and the GNN reached 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond inference on the tested planar tactile structure.
infographic.watch_item: Results are demonstrated on a 2D planar tactile setup, so transfer to more complex 3D sensors or unseen material behaviors may require revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: FEM-Validated Real-Time Modelling of Soft Tactile Deformation

title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression
authors: Nikolaos Kegkeroglou, Bilal Sabillah, Myrto Inglezou, Vincent Placet, Céndric Clevy, Antonios Porichis
abstract: Plant fibers are increasingly used as sustainable reinforcements in composites, but the intrinsic variability of their microstructure causes substantial scatter in transverse mechanical behavior, complicating composite design. Characterizing this behavior relies on finite element (FE) simulations requiring several minutes of high-performance computing per fiber, making high-throughput characterization across realistic fiber populations impractical. In this study, we propose a deep learning framework replacing this FE bottleneck with a fast pipeline. It includes two coupled recursive U-Nets predicting the step-by-step evolution of fiber deformation and internal stress fields under transverse compression, followed by a regression CNN estimating the transverse Young's modulus from the final stress field. Unlike prior approaches predicting stress fields for fixed configurations or idealized geometries, our framework recursively resolves the full temporal stress evolution for synthetic fibers derived from real hemp cross-sections, with or without a lumen. Trained on 1,000 synthetic fiber geometries with FE ground truth, it reproduces the stress field sequence with a Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) of $0.9574 \pm 0.0074$ and a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of $0.0345 \pm 0.0079$. It estimates transverse Young's modulus with an $R^2$ of $0.938 \pm 0.024$, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of $24.31 \pm 1.23$ MPa, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of $5.25 \pm 0.91\%$. Inference requires under one second per fiber versus five minutes per FE simulation, drastically reducing computational cost. This offers a fast, reliable tool for mechanical characterization of synthetic plant fibers, with promising applications in designing natural fiber-reinforced composites.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive deep-learning pipeline can replace slow finite-element simulation to predict the full transverse-compression response of synthetic plant fibers and estimate their effective stiffness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables high-throughput mechanical characterization of variable natural-fiber microstructures, supporting faster design of sustainable fiber-reinforced composites.
method: Train two coupled recursive U-Nets to propagate deformation and stress fields step by step under transverse compression.
Use a regression CNN on the final stress field to predict transverse Young’s modulus.
Train and validate on 1,000 synthetic hemp-like fiber geometries with FE ground truth, including cases with and without a lumen.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model achieved SSIM 0.9574 ± 0.0074 and RMSE 0.0345 ± 0.0079 for stress-field evolution, and predicted Young’s modulus with R² = 0.938 ± 0.024, MAE = 24.31 ± 1.23 MPa, and MAPE = 5.25 ± 0.91%, while inference took under one second versus about five minutes for FE.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on synthetic geometries derived from hemp cross-sections, so robustness on unseen real fibers, broader loading conditions, or manufacturing variability still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning-based Mechanical Characterization of Synthetically Generated Plant Fibers under Transverse Compression

title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners
authors: Filipe Cumaru, Hadi Hajibeygi, Cornelis Vuik, Alexander Heinlein
abstract: The robustness of two-level overlapping additive Schwarz (OAS) preconditioners for highly heterogeneous elliptic problems hinges on the choice of the coarse space. We propose an algebraic multiscale (AM) coarse space built from the system matrix alone through an algebraic formulation of the multiscale finite element method (MsFEM). The coarse basis functions are energy-minimizing extensions of the solutions of reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on the subdomain interface, so that coefficient variations along the interface enter the coarse space. By posing the RBC problems on slabs that extend the interface, the construction also applies to general unstructured domain decompositions. Embedding the AM formulation in an energy-minimizing framework extends it to linear elasticity, and we show that existing condition number bounds for OAS with MsFEM coarse spaces carry over to the algebraic setting. For problems with high coefficient inclusions on the coarse nodes, the AM iteration count and condition number are unaffected by increasing the contrast. In 3D scalar diffusion with log-normal coefficients, AM needs about as many iterations as the generalized Dryja--Smith--Widlund (GDSW) coarse space, while solving a coarse problem ten times smaller. For linear elasticity, omitting the coarse basis functions associated with the rotational rigid body modes yields a fully algebraic coarse space that still scales well for homogeneous problems.

infographic.key_insight: An algebraic multiscale coarse space built from interface-based reduced boundary condition problems can make two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners robust to strong coefficient heterogeneity while staying fully matrix-based.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a practical, scalable preconditioning strategy for large heterogeneous elliptic and elasticity problems, especially when geometric multiscale information is unavailable.
method: Construct coarse basis functions by solving algebraic reduced boundary condition problems on interface slabs.
Use energy-minimizing extensions so coefficient variations along interfaces are captured in the coarse space.
Embed the approach in an energy-minimizing framework to extend it from scalar diffusion to linear elasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the method stays contrast-robust when high-coefficient inclusions sit on coarse nodes, matches GDSW iteration counts in 3D log-normal diffusion, and uses a coarse problem about ten times smaller.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on how well the interface/slab construction captures the relevant heterogeneity, and elasticity requires careful handling of rigid body modes.
infographic.paper_title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

infographic.key_insight: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW and RGDSW coarse spaces remain robust for high-order 2D FEM/VEM Poisson solves, while RGDSW cuts coarse-space size substantially.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These preconditioners support scalable high-order discretizations by improving solver robustness and reducing coarse-problem cost in large finite element and virtual element simulations.
method: Use additive Schwarz with overlap and a two-level coarse correction.
Compare GDSW against reduced GDSW coarse spaces for conforming Pk and Qk FEM.
Extend the same preconditioning strategy to polygonal-mesh VEM in 2D.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical condition-number bounds and numerical tests on structured triangular, quadrilateral, and polygonal meshes up to polynomial degree k=9, with RGDSW reducing coarse dimension by about 3x while keeping competitive iteration counts.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is shown for selected polynomial orders and 2D Poisson problems, so behavior on more complex PDEs, 3D geometries, or less favorable mesh/interface conditions may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D

title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations
authors: Joy Saha, Jun Yang, Peimeng Yin
abstract: In this work, we develop low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations and incorporate them into a basis-update \& Galerkin mass-lumped finite element method (\mbox{BUG-MLFEM}). By incorporating mass lumping via Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, the spatial discretization yields a matrix differential equation equipped with diagonal positive-definite mass matrices. We establish the weighted dynamical low-rank approximation (WDLRA) within the Galerkin framework of the MLFEM system, proving the theoretical equivalence between the BUG integrator and MLFEM on low-rank subspaces, which guarantees the discrete well-posedness of the implicit BUG steps. To overcome the severe computational bottleneck of standard $O(m^3+n^3)$ Sylvester solvers, we develop tailored, low-cost non-iterative solvers that exploit the inherent sparse-by-small algebraic structure. Under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions (BCs), the large coefficient matrices are banded, enabling efficient diagonalization of the small $r \times r$ factor matrix and reducing the per-step computational complexity to $O((m+n)r^2)$ and storage to $O((m+n)r)$. For periodic BCs, we combine this diagonalization strategy with a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update to handle wrap-around corner entries at negligible additional cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate first-order temporal and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence of the proposed BUG-MLFEM in the discrete $L^2$ norm, where $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the finite element space, together with significant computational speedups over existing low-rank integrators.

infographic.key_insight: The paper couples mass-lumped finite elements with weighted dynamical low-rank approximation to solve reaction-diffusion systems efficiently using low-cost, non-iterative Sylvester solvers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, memory-light reduced-order simulation of PDEs, making implicit low-rank integrators more practical for large-scale engineering discretizations.
method: Use BUG-MLFEM with Gauss-Lobatto mass lumping to obtain diagonal positive-definite mass matrices.
Formulate the low-rank evolution in a Galerkin weighted dynamical low-rank framework and solve the Sylvester subproblems non-iteratively.
Exploit banded structure for Dirichlet/Neumann BCs and use a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update for periodic BCs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports first-order temporal and (k+1)th-order spatial convergence in discrete L2 norm, along with significant speedups over existing low-rank integrators.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on structured sparse matrices and low-rank assumptions, so the approach may be less effective for highly irregular meshes, strongly nonlinear regimes, or problems that do not preserve low-rank structure.
infographic.paper_title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations

title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
authors: Jin Liu, Ning Xi, Yinbin Miao, Junkang Liu, Ke Cheng, Jianfeng Ma
abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.

infographic.key_insight: DP-SPA improves continual LoRA under differential privacy by separating stable and plastic subspaces, which reduces forgetting while preserving adaptation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical privacy-preserving fine-tuning strategy for engineering and scientific models that must learn from sequential sensitive datasets without catastrophic performance loss.
method: Build a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from the orthogonal complement of pretrained weights.
Fix these bases and privately optimize only one LoRA factor to remove bilinear noise interaction in each update.
Rescale stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies before merging task updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments on five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets, with improved average accuracy and reduced forgetting versus baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurate subspace construction and coefficient recalibration, which may add implementation complexity and could be sensitive to task sequence or low-signal updates.
infographic.paper_title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA

title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
authors: Yue Wu, Haoyu Wan, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

infographic.key_insight: Specialized, physics-informed machine learning force fields are needed to reliably simulate complex materials dynamics because general pretrained ML potentials often fail on highly strained, reactive, or nonlocal out-of-distribution states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For fracture, damage, and other extreme loading problems, the key takeaway is that force fields should be tailored and validated against the specific observables and regimes engineers actually care about.
method: Compare universal foundation models with task-specific potentials
Use physics-driven specialization for difficult dynamical settings
Benchmark models by observable-specific performance in target applications
infographic.evidence_signal: The review synthesizes evidence across four demanding contexts—electrified interfaces, open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture—to assess where standard MLIPs break down and where specialized models help.
infographic.watch_item: Specialization can improve fidelity, but it must be carefully benchmarked because added architectural complexity, nonlocal terms, and scaling costs may limit practicality in large simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics

title: Data-Driven Discovery of a Hyperelastic Strain-Energy Function for Veins Using Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks
authors: Marisa Bazzi, Divya Adil, Gavin Mays, Ellen Kuhl, Christopher K. Breuer, Jay D. Humphrey
abstract: Veins are commonly subjected to altered mechanical loading in clinical settings such as vein grafting, arteriovenous fistula creation, and tissue-engineered vascular graft implantation, making accurate constitutive models of venous tissue clinically important. Venous mechanical behavior differs characteristically from that of arteries, and existing constitutive models struggle to simultaneously fit the circumferential and axial stress-stretch responses across vein types. Here, we present a constitutive artificial neural network (CANN) framework that discovers a compact, interpretable hyperelastic constitutive model from biaxial mechanical data across three types of veins (saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava). The framework incorporates an expanded candidate function library with structurally motivated terms representing progressive fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions. Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation-based pruning, and response-level family collapse were then used to reduce the discovered basis to a compact strain-energy density function (SEF). The resulting eight-term SEF achieved significantly higher fitting accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three types of veins $(R^2>0.9, p<0.01)$. These findings establish a framework for constitutive model discovery in veins and propose a candidate constitutive form for further validation across larger, independent cohorts.

infographic.key_insight: A constitutive artificial neural network discovered a compact, interpretable hyperelastic strain-energy function for veins that captures biaxial mechanical behavior better than standard vein models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a data-driven constitutive law that could improve simulation and design for vein grafts, arteriovenous fistulas, and tissue-engineered vascular grafts.
method: Fit a CANN to biaxial stress-stretch data from saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava veins.
Expand the candidate function library with terms for fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions.
Use Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation pruning, and response-level family collapse to reduce the model to an 8-term SEF.
infographic.evidence_signal: The final eight-term strain-energy function achieved higher accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three vein types, with R² > 0.9 and p < 0.01.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed constitutive form should be validated on larger, independent cohorts before broad clinical or design use.
infographic.paper_title: Data-Driven Discovery of a Hyperelastic Strain-Energy Function for Veins Using Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks

title: Efficient Shallow Ritz Method: 1D Semi-Linear Diffusion-Reaction and Allen-Cahn Equations
authors: Zhiqiang Cai, César Herrera
abstract: An efficient shallow Ritz method was developed in [8, 9] for one-dimensional linear diffusion and diffusion-reaction problems. In this paper, the method is extended to a nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation with a cubic reaction term: (1) a basic error estimate of the shallow Ritz discretization is established and (2) a reduced block Newton (rBN) method for solving the resulting non-convex optimization problem is developed. Again, the computational cost of the rBN method is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ for one-dimensional problems, where $n$ is the number of neurons. Combining a convex splitting scheme for time discretization with the efficient shallow Ritz method, we develop a time-stepping neural network method for solving the Allen-Cahn equation. The unconditional energy stability of the time discretization and an error estimate in the $L^2$ norm are established. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the neural network approach yields accurate solutions for singularly perturbed nonlinear diffusion-reaction equations and the Allen-Cahn equation. The method effectively resolves interior and boundary layers without oscillations and significantly outperforms the finite element method on fixed uniform meshes.

infographic.key_insight: A shallow Ritz neural network can efficiently solve 1D nonlinear diffusion-reaction and Allen-Cahn problems with O(n) optimization cost while preserving accuracy and stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a fast FEM surrogate for stiff, singularly perturbed PDEs that captures boundary/interior layers on fixed meshes better than standard finite elements.
method: Use a shallow Ritz discretization for the nonlinear variational form.
Solve the resulting non-convex training problem with a reduced block Newton (rBN) method in O(n) per iteration for 1D.
Combine convex splitting in time with the shallow Ritz solver for an energy-stable Allen-Cahn time-stepping scheme.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments showing accurate layer resolution without oscillations, plus theoretical error estimates and unconditional energy stability.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and O(n) scalability are demonstrated for one-dimensional settings, so extension to higher-dimensional or more complex geometries may require additional algorithmic care.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Shallow Ritz Method: 1D Semi-Linear Diffusion-Reaction and Allen-Cahn Equations

title: Force Sensor-Based Picking Pattern Analysis and Two-Jaw Gripper Design for Cherry Tomato Robotic Harvesting in Greenhouse
authors: Rajmeet Singh, Manveen Kaur, Yusuf Adamu, Irfan Hussain
abstract: Robotic harvesting of cherry tomatoes in greenhouses remains challenging due to dense fruit clusters, delicate skin, and the need for gentle yet effective detachment. This study presents a force-data-driven framework for autonomous cherry tomato harvesting that integrates six-axis force/torque sensing, a bio-inspired compliant gripper, and deployment on a mobile robotic platform. A wearable ATI six-axis force/torque sensor mounted on the index finger captured kinetic signatures of three elemental picking patterns (gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling) across 150 manual trials (50 per pattern) in laboratory and greenhouse settings. Gripping required a peak normal force of 3.92 and 0.45 N, twisting produced a dominant torque of 19.20 2.10 Nmm about the pedicel axis with minimal truss disturbance, and pure lateral pulling alone was insufficient for reliable detachment. These measurements informed a novel fingertip-localised Finray gripper, with compliant TPU 95A Finray geometry restricted to the fruit-contact region and a rigid PLA body, emulating the dual-stiffness human fingertip. A Dynamixel XM430-W350 servomotor under current-based torque control applies the measured gripping force and a 45° wrist twist. Finite element analysis showed a maximum von Mises stress of 0.24 MPa under the 3.92 N load, below the bruising threshold of cherry tomato skin. Integrated on a UR5 arm and Clearpath Husky A200 base, the system was validated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and in 50 autonomous trials at the SILAL commercial greenhouse, Abu Dhabi, UAE. The hybrid grip-twist-pull strategy achieved an 86.0% picking success rate, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4 s cycle time per fruit, outperforming vacuum (66.3%), rotating (70.1%), clamping (76.0%), and suction-cutting (52.4%) end-effectors. These results demonstrate preliminary feasibility under the tested facility and cultivar conditions

infographic.key_insight: Cherry tomato detachment is most reliable when a compliant fingertip gripper combines measured gripping force with a controlled wrist twist, rather than relying on pulling alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper translates human picking force signatures into a bio-inspired gripper design that balances detachment success with fruit-skin safety for greenhouse robotics.
method: Captured six-axis force/torque data from 150 manual picking trials for gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling.
Used the measured force/torque signatures to design a dual-stiffness Finray fingertip gripper with TPU contact regions and a rigid PLA body.
Validated the hybrid grip-twist-pull strategy on a UR5-Husky platform in simulation and 50 greenhouse trials.
infographic.evidence_signal: The autonomous system achieved 86.0% picking success, 2.3% fruit damage, and 8.4 s per fruit, outperforming several alternative end-effectors.
infographic.watch_item: Results were demonstrated for one greenhouse setup and cultivar, so performance may vary with fruit size, cluster density, and field conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Force Sensor-Based Picking Pattern Analysis and Two-Jaw Gripper Design for Cherry Tomato Robotic Harvesting in Greenhouse

title: DexNinja: Learning Robust Dexterous Cutting Policy with a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Engine
authors: Haozhe Lou, Runyi Yang, Wanqi Zhong, Caiyun Liu, Yicheng Liu, Wenhao Liu
abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates or damages the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting is expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elasticity responses quickly compound. We propose \textsc{DexNinja}, a real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. \textsc{DexNinja} (i) reconstructs object instances from real captures, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters under category-level constraints, and (iii) produces augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate \textsc{DexNinja} on a dexterous food-slicing task and show that (1) with tens of real demonstrations and hundreds of augmented simulator data, the success rate could reach more than 60\%. (2) the augmented data consistently improves success rates when only using real data with more than 20\% via sim-to-real, and (3) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects with varying shapes and sizes.

infographic.key_insight: DexNinja learns robust dexterous cutting by converting a small number of real demonstrations into a much denser, physically plausible real-to-sim-to-real training set.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces the data cost of training robotic manipulation policies for deformable, topology-changing materials such as food while improving transfer from simulation to real hardware.
method: Reconstructs food object instances from real captures to build realistic initial states.
Randomizes physically meaningful material and contact parameters under category-level constraints.
Generates augmented cutting episodes with a custom differentiable simulator coupling robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using tens of real demonstrations plus hundreds of augmented simulation samples, the policy achieved over 60% success and improved real-only training by more than 20% via sim-to-real augmentation.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on simulator fidelity for contact, friction, and cutting physics, which are difficult to model accurately for varied deformable foods.
infographic.paper_title: DexNinja: Learning Robust Dexterous Cutting Policy with a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Engine

title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
authors: Federica Milinanni, Andrei Kramer-Miehe, Jan Glaubitz, Olivia Eriksson
abstract: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.

infographic.key_insight: Thermodynamic consistency in biochemical reaction-network inference can be encouraged by penalizing detailed-balance violations instead of explicitly enforcing Wegscheider constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a more scalable and numerically stable way to calibrate physically grounded reaction models, especially when Bayesian inference and complex network topologies make direct constraint handling difficult.
method: Infer network parameters with a penalty term that discourages detailed-balance violations.
Avoid explicit cycle identification and reparameterization needed for direct Wegscheider enforcement.
Apply and test the approach on both a single-cycle toy network and a PKA-calcineurin signaling model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that unconstrained inference fit the data but violated thermodynamic constraints, while the proposed penalty preserved data agreement and produced posterior samples that approximately satisfied detailed balance.
infographic.watch_item: Because the constraint is enforced approximately rather than exactly, the penalty strength must be tuned carefully to balance physical consistency against fit quality and sampling performance.
infographic.paper_title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks

title: First-fracture kinetics in periodic chains: from free-energy landscapes and dynamical recrossing to absolute rates
authors: Aristotelis P. Sgouros
abstract: The nearly collinear configuration of highly stretched polymer chains before fracture motivates one-dimensional models. At fixed extension, stretching one bond redistributes length among the others, coupling rupture to the whole chain. In this work, I develop a framework for fracture-healing rates in periodic Morse chains, combining deterministic theories, equilibrium simulations and a quasi-deterministic approach using equilibrium fluxes and barrier-top trajectories. Constrained-partition calculations closely reproduce simulated populations and intact-state tensions. An intact-reservoir potential of mean force (PMF) supplies the first-fracture surface probability, while recrossing corrects the attempt flux without a rate-fitted prefactor. Independent rate tests identify an operational chain-length boundary for accurate two-state kinetics; failed-return durations decrease relative to population relaxation as chains grow. Kramers-Grote-Hynes (KGH), nonlinear reactive-flux and equilibrium rates show excellent agreement in this regime. KGH predicts rates away from coexistence and a chain-dependent local activation length dominated by the barrier response. Rates decrease approximately exponentially before declining more gently for longer chains: barrier growth dominates, additional fracture sites partly compensate, and transmission varies more weakly. Beyond coexistence, long chains can fracture practically irreversibly because healing becomes too rare to observe. Projected committor crossings, where the configuration-averaged probability of reaching the fractured core first is one half, lie near site-PMF maxima, although configurations at equal bond length retain different fracture probabilities. Multiple fractures remain negligible near coexistence through at least $N=50$. The framework could supply state-dependent rates to mesoscopic fracture models of polymer networks.

infographic.key_insight: First-fracture in stretched periodic polymer chains is governed by a chain-coupled free-energy landscape, where barrier growth and dynamical recrossing together set the absolute rate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a rate-predictive framework for polymer fracture and healing that can feed mesoscopic damage models of networks and highly stretched materials.
method: Constrained-partition calculations for intact-chain populations and tensions
Intact-reservoir PMF to estimate first-fracture surface probabilities
Kramers-Grote-Hynes, nonlinear reactive-flux, and quasi-deterministic barrier-top trajectory analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: The theoretical rates and populations closely match equilibrium simulations, and several independent rate tests show good agreement up to an operational chain-length limit.
infographic.watch_item: Two-state kinetics becomes unreliable for longer chains where healing is too rare and multiple-fracture effects may start to matter, especially beyond coexistence.
infographic.paper_title: First-fracture kinetics in periodic chains: from free-energy landscapes and dynamical recrossing to absolute rates

title: Analytical and numerical periodic homogenization of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations in a $W^{2,p}$ Cordes framework
authors: Timo Sprekeler, Hung V. Tran
abstract: We study periodic homogenization of fully-nonlinear second-order Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations subject to a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition and the numerical approximation of the effective Hamiltonian, where the diffusion matrix is assumed to satisfy the Cordes condition. In the first part, assuming the Cordes parameter is sufficiently large, we show existence and uniqueness of $W^{2,p}$ solutions to the true cell problem, prove homogenization under minimal regularity assumptions, and establish a quantitative homogenization result. In the second part, we propose and rigorously analyze $W^{2,p}$-conforming and mixed finite element methods for the approximation of the corrector, which are then used in the approximation of the effective Hamiltonian. The key tool used throughout this work is Campanato's concept of near operators.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that periodic homogenization for fully nonlinear HJB/Isaacs equations can be made analytically well-posed and numerically tractable in a $W^{2,p}$ Cordes setting, enabling reliable approximation of the effective Hamiltonian.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives computational mechanics and multiscale PDE solvers a rigorous route to replace oscillatory microstructure models with effective coarse-scale operators while retaining accuracy guarantees.
method: Prove existence and uniqueness of $W^{2,p}$ cell-problem solutions under a sufficiently strong Cordes condition.
Establish periodic homogenization and a quantitative error result with minimal regularity assumptions.
Develop and analyze $W^{2,p}$-conforming and mixed finite element schemes to compute correctors and the effective Hamiltonian.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results and rigorous finite element analysis, including existence/uniqueness, homogenization, and quantitative convergence, rather than numerical benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: The framework relies on a sufficiently large Cordes parameter and specialized $W^{2,p}$-conforming/mixed discretizations, so applicability may be limited when these conditions are hard to verify or enforce in practice.
infographic.paper_title: Analytical and numerical periodic homogenization of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations in a $W^{2,p}$ Cordes framework

title: POD-accelerated high-order multiscale method with corrected-basis reconstruction for transient multi-continuum problems
authors: Jiayuan Peng, Hao Dong, Jiale Linghu
abstract: Multi-continuum models provide an effective macroscopic description of transient flow in fractured and highly heterogeneous porous media by introducing several interacting state variables at each macroscale location. Although high-order multiscale (HOMS) methods reduce the cost of resolving microscopic heterogeneities while recovering local oscillatory features, repeated solution of the coupled homogenized system and repeated high-order reconstruction remain expensive in long-time and large-scale three-dimensional simulations. This work develops a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) accelerated HOMS framework for transient multi-continuum problems. A vector-valued POD space is constructed from snapshots of the coupled homogenized solution, and the resulting block system is projected onto a low-dimensional space. Two recovery strategies are considered. The first reconstructs the reduced homogenized fields and performs full HOMS assembly at every output time. The second applies the spatial part of the multiscale recovery operator to retained POD modes offline and evaluates the online solution by direct linear combinations of corrected bases and time-derivative bases. An error estimate between the fully discrete homogenized solution and its POD-reduced approximation is established for the coupled system. A recovered POD-HOMS estimate is then obtained by combining the HOMS consistency error with POD truncation errors propagated through value, gradient, inter-continuum exchange, second-derivative, and time-derivative recovery terms. Numerical experiments for two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous configurations show that the reduced solutions retain the accuracy and local oscillatory behavior of the corresponding HOMS solution while substantially decreasing computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: The paper combines POD model reduction with high-order multiscale reconstruction to make transient multi-continuum fracture/porous-media simulations much cheaper while preserving HOMS-level accuracy and oscillatory detail.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster large-scale 2D/3D simulations of fractured and highly heterogeneous media, which is valuable for subsurface flow, transport, and damage-related multiphysics applications.
method: Build a vector-valued POD space from snapshots of the coupled homogenized multi-continuum system.
Project the block homogenized equations onto a low-dimensional reduced basis.
Use either online HOMS reassembly or offline corrected-basis reconstruction with recovered value, gradient, exchange, second-derivative, and time-derivative terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical error estimates and numerical tests in two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous cases showing reduced solutions preserve HOMS accuracy and local oscillations while lowering cost.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the representativeness of POD snapshots and the overhead of constructing/applying corrected bases for new parameter regimes or long-time dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: POD-accelerated high-order multiscale method with corrected-basis reconstruction for transient multi-continuum problems

title: Least-Squares Finite Element Methods with Weakly Imposed Boundary Conditions: Norm and Error Equivalences, Over-Penalization, and Fully Discontinuous Discretizations
authors: Shun Zhang
abstract: Weakly imposed boundary conditions in first-order system least-squares methods go back to Jespersen (1977), but two questions have remained open for decades: the right weights, especially for the Neumann residual, whose natural norm $H^{-1/2}$ suggests $h_F$, and norm and error equivalences, especially for indefinite equations. We answer both for general, possibly indefinite, second-order elliptic equations with non-homogeneous mixed boundary conditions. First, for the weights $h_F^{-1}$ on the Dirichlet and $1$ on the Neumann residual, we prove norm and error equivalences with mesh-independent constants for every discrete pair: the error in a mesh-dependent norm is equivalent to the square root of the functional plus a Dirichlet data term. The least-squares solution converges optimally in $H(\mathrm{div};Ω)\times H^{1}(Ω)$, and the functional is a reliable and efficient error estimator, with a recovered flux also for approximations from other methods, even ones violating the boundary conditions. The key idea is to apply the stability of the boundary value problem to pairs that are discrete only in their Dirichlet traces, whose $H^{1/2}$ norm an inverse inequality bounds by the weighted penalty. Second, these weights are the right ones: weaker powers, including $h_F$ on the Neumann boundary, destroy the norm equivalence, and stronger weights are admissible, since the penalty multiplies zero at a comparison function meeting the projected data. Third, for the fully discontinuous counterpart, a pure penalty method with both jumps weighted by $h_F^{-1}$, the error equivalence holds for every discrete pair, also for exact fluxes with normal traces not square integrable on interior faces.

infographic.key_insight: For least-squares FEM with weak boundary conditions, the correct penalty scaling is h_F^{-1} on Dirichlet terms and 1 on Neumann terms, yielding mesh-independent norm and error equivalence even for indefinite elliptic problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a reliable a posteriori error estimator and robust recovered fluxes for mixed-boundary PDEs, including when boundary conditions are only weakly satisfied or the discretization is fully discontinuous.
method: Prove norm/error equivalence in a mesh-dependent least-squares norm.
Use inverse inequalities on discrete Dirichlet traces plus stability of the continuous boundary value problem.
Extend to a discontinuous penalty formulation with h_F^{-1} weights on both jumps.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytic equivalence results with mesh-independent constants and optimal convergence, rather than numerical experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Using weaker Neumann weighting (e.g., h_F) breaks the equivalence, so implementation must respect the proposed scaling to retain reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Least-Squares Finite Element Methods with Weakly Imposed Boundary Conditions: Norm and Error Equivalences, Over-Penalization, and Fully Discontinuous Discretizations
